profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting for a two-week sprint to prepare a DREAM workshop submission. The team has already validated the high-level research idea, and this meeting is to decide how to run a small pilot evaluation, which benchmark slice to use, what the verification component should cover, how to split writing responsibilities, and what must be ready by the internal draft deadline. The expected outcome is an agreed plan for the pilot run, dataset/version to use, ownership of experimental and writing tasks, and a timeline leading to a draft the following Friday.

members.name: Dr. Lena Park
members.expertise: LLM evaluation, benchmark design, research framing
members.background: An assistant professor leading a lab on evaluation methods for agentic language systems; she typically focuses on paper positioning, taxonomy design, and which empirical evidence is sufficient for a convincing workshop submission.
members.private_state: She wants a clean, defensible pilot that can be turned into a credible workshop paper quickly, and she is worried that infrastructure-heavy extensions will slow the submission and produce results that are harder to narrate cleanly.
hidden_assumptions: When she says a pilot uses '12 queries,' she means 12 standalone evaluation prompts total, not prompt families expanded across temporal variants.
A benchmark slice referred to by month is assumed to be a frozen export suitable for reproducible tables, not a live folder that may have been refreshed.
A 'verification pass' means checking factual and temporal correctness of claims surfaced in the final report, not auditing the entire search process that produced the report.
A 'draft' due Friday is something she can circulate to coauthors immediately, with stable figures, tables, and prose rather than placeholders.
Internal deadlines are oriented around when she can read and comment during the workday, not merely when files exist somewhere in the repo.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.expertise: evaluation pipelines, agent tooling, benchmark automation
members.background: A senior research engineer who built much of the lab's benchmarking infrastructure and usually translates research ideas into runnable evaluation pipelines, data jobs, and analysis notebooks.
members.private_state: He wants to reuse the existing infrastructure efficiently, avoid manual benchmark curation, and make sure the evaluation setup reflects the full behavior of research agents rather than a narrow post-hoc checker.
hidden_assumptions: In the existing harness, one 'query' is a research question bundle that can include multiple temporal variants, so '12 queries' naturally includes those linked variants.
The cloud storage folder currently labeled 'april_slice' is the authoritative version unless someone explicitly asks for an older frozen export.

A proper 'verification pass' should inspect retrieval behavior and missed-source cases, because factual correctness depends on whether the agent searched adequately, not only on whether cited claims look true afterward.
A 'draft' means a structured manuscript with provisional numbers and placeholders that can be iterated on after feedback.
Lab deadlines usually mean end of engineer workday or overnight job completion, since analysis artifacts often land late and get reviewed the next morning.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as '12 queries' in the pilot
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'start with a 12-query pilot.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means 12 total report-generation tasks, chosen to be representative across the taxonomy, with no automatic expansion into additional temporal versions during the pilot.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means 12 benchmark query bundles from the harness, each already linked to temporal variants, so the pilot would actually execute multiple report-generation runs per bundle.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both see themselves as proposing a small pilot, and internally the team often uses 'query' loosely; the expansion into temporal variants is embedded in the tooling rather than treated as a separate planning decision.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'April benchmark slice' they will run
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to using 'the April benchmark slice.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the frozen 180-query export assembled before the most recent crawler refresh, because it is the stable slice she expects for reproducible paper tables.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the current cloud folder named 'april_slice,' whose contents were partially refreshed after a crawler rerun but kept the same label for compatibility with existing jobs.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The shared label makes the reference feel unambiguous, and both assume versioning conventions are already understood, so neither thinks to specify timestamps or storage paths.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the pilot should include a 'verification pass.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a post-generation checker that verifies factual claims, citations, and dates appearing in the final report.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means an end-to-end audit that also replays tool traces and flags whether the agent's search process failed to retrieve obvious necessary sources.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both uses fit naturally under the phrase 'verification pass,' and both are plausibly part of evaluating research quality, so the difference feels like implementation detail rather than a separate scope decision.

misalignment_points.topic: What qualifies as a 'draft by next Friday'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to have 'a draft by next Friday.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a coauthor-ready workshop draft with stable tables and figures, enough to circulate externally within the lab network that same afternoon.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means an Overleaf manuscript skeleton with method text, preliminary plots, and provisional numbers that can still change after overnight reruns.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In research teams, 'draft' is commonly used for anything from a polished paper version to a structured placeholder document, and both assume their lab's norm is obvious without restating it.

turns.inner_thought: We already know the high-level story is viable; what I need now is a tight sprint that yields a clean pilot and a narratable workshop paper. The biggest risk is letting this balloon into infrastructure work or a sprawling evaluation that muddies the framing. I want concrete ownership, a modest pilot, stable outputs, and enough polish that I can circulate the paper internally without apologizing for placeholders.
turns.utterance: Okay, let's make this concrete. We have two weeks, the idea is already in decent shape, and what we need now is a plan that gets the DREAM pilot running and turns into a workshop write-up without too much drift. I'd like us to leave with the pilot scope, the benchmark slice, who owns what, and what has to be ready for the internal deadline.

turns.inner_thought: This should be straightforward if we stay close to the existing pipeline. I can point the harness at the cloud folder labeled april_slice and avoid any manual curation. As long as nobody asks for some older archived export, the current folder is the authoritative April benchmark slice in practice, and reusing it will save us a lot of setup time.
turns.utterance: That sounds good. On the execution side, I can reuse the existing harness, so we shouldn't need much custom setup. If we start from the April benchmark slice, I can get something running pretty quickly.

turns.inner_thought: I want this pilot genuinely small: 12 standalone report-generation tasks total, handpicked to cover the taxonomy and show whether the adaptive metrics catch Mirage-of-Synthesis behavior. Not expanded families, not a bunch of variants hiding inside the word query. Twelve total should be enough to sanity-check the signal without creating a huge analysis burden.
turns.utterance: Great. For the pilot itself, I'd really like to start with a 12-query pilot and use that to sanity-check whether the adaptive metrics are actually exposing the Mirage-of-Synthesis failures we care about before we scale anything up.

turns.inner_thought: Twelve queries is a nice small pilot in harness terms. Since each query bundle already carries the linked temporal variants, I can get comparisons across those conditions almost for free. That's actually ideal: we keep the nominal pilot small while still seeing how behavior shifts over time without designing a second experiment.
turns.utterance: Yeah, that makes sense. Using those 12 queries with the harness should let me get the temporal comparisons running almost immediately, which is a nice way to make the pilot informative without a lot of extra machinery.

turns.inner_thought: I also need the evaluation to look responsible, especially because the paper is about research quality. By verification pass, I mean a post-generation check on the final reports: are the time-sensitive claims right, do the citations support what's written, and are dates and factual statements defensible? I do not want this to turn into auditing every search step the agent took.
turns.utterance: And I do think the pilot should include a verification pass, especially around whether the generated reports hold up on time-sensitive claims and citation-grounded statements. If that part looks weak, the rest of the framing is going to be hard to defend.

turns.inner_thought: Good, verification should be end-to-end. If I replay the tool traces and flag missed-source cases, we'll capture whether the agent failed because it never retrieved necessary evidence, not just whether the final text sounds wrong. That's a more faithful measure of research behavior, and I can integrate it into the existing logging stack.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I'll make the verification pass replay the agent's tool traces and flag missed-source situations too, so the scoring reflects retrieval quality and not just the final write-up.

turns.inner_thought: As long as the frozen April export behaves cleanly, the rest is mostly packaging: convert the pilot into a few stable tables, a compact framing, and a coauthor-ready draft I can circulate next Friday afternoon. I need figures and prose that are stable enough to read in one pass, not a shell document that still depends on overnight reruns.
turns.utterance: Right. If the April benchmark slice behaves cleanly, then the main remaining milestone is really turning the pilot into tables and a draft by next Friday. That's the point where I want us shifting from setup mode into paper mode.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. I'll rerun the current april_slice job tonight, let the jobs finish overnight, and by Friday I can push the numbers and a structured Overleaf draft with the method and results scaffolding in place. The plots may still move a bit after reruns, but that's normal; we'll iterate once Lena comments.
turns.utterance: Yep, that works. I'll rerun the april_slice job overnight and push the numbers plus an Overleaf structure by Friday, so we have something concrete to work from.

turns.inner_thought: I'll take the parts that shape the submission story: framing, taxonomy, related work, why Mirage-of-Synthesis matters, and how the pilot supports the claim. Arjun should own the methods and results text since he'll have the implementation details and outputs. If he gives me stable figures and tables by Friday, I can stitch everything into a strong workshop draft quickly.
turns.utterance: Let me take the framing, related-work positioning, and the taxonomy sections. If you can own the methods, pilot results, and implementation notes, that should split things cleanly and keep the writing moving in parallel.

turns.inner_thought: That division is good. I'll wire the pilot through the harness, run the verification pass in the fuller sense, keep the logs and traces organized, and leave enough infrastructure in place that we can extend beyond the initial 12 query bundles after the first draft lands. As usual, I'll probably have artifacts landing late, but by next morning there should be enough in Overleaf and the repo to iterate.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll wire up the pilot, run the verification pass, and keep detailed logs so we have a clean record of what happened and can extend the setup after the initial draft.
